title: Drive vs. Decay: On the Training Dynamics of Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
claim: Competing drive and decay forces define a phase boundary separating a learning regime from a collapse regime across control mechanisms.
layout: single heatmap panel, formula box on top, annotated regions with arrows, red boundary contour
description: A single square heatmap with a hand-drawn, sketchy style. The x-axis is 'Example Mechanism 1: Predictor Scale' and the y-axis is 'Example Mechanism 2: Context Ratio'. The background shades from dark green on the left through pale yellow in the middle to dark red on the right. Near-vertical contour lines are labelled μ=5.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5 and 0.1. The μ=1.0 line is thick red and marks the phase boundary. A red-bordered box above the plot gives the formula μ = drive(γ)/decay(σ) = 1. A rounded box on the left reads 'Learning: γ > σ', with a red arrow pointing left from the boundary. A box at lower right reads 'Collapse: γ < σ', with a red arrow pointing right. The eye goes first to the formula box, then to the red boundary line splitting the green and red regions.
caption: Phase boundary. Learning where the drive wins (µ = γ/σ > 1), collapse where the decay wins (µ < 1).
abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are prone to representation collapse, typically mitigated through empirical heuristics. We develop an early-training stability theory that unifies these heuristics. Linearising the coupled JEPA gradient flow around the trivial fixed point reveals two competing effects: a driving force ($Î³$) and a decay effect ($Ï$). Under approximate spectral decoupling, a per-mode stability ratio $Î¼_i = Î³_i / Ï_i$ factorises into independent data-side and predictor-side terms and the count of unstable modes tracks the rank of representations that can emerge. The framework predicts a phase boundary, which we confirm empirically across more than 800 Tabular-JEPA configurations. It also unifies predictor scaling, masking ratio, and EMA as distinct mechanisms for shifting $Î¼$. Guided by this analysis, we introduce ResidualPred, a transformer predictor whose attention is biased toward the identity at initialisation; it improves both effective rank and downstream accuracy on tabular benchmarks and in I-JEPA pretraining on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, and ImageNet. Our framework connects empirical collapse-avoidance heuristics to an explicit dynamical picture, yielding theory-driven stabilizers. Code is available at https://github.com/jose-melo/drive-vs-decay.
